harbinger

/HAR-bin-jer/ - the stress falls on HAR · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Harbinger means a sign that something is coming.

In the orchard, the first windfall apples are a harbinger of the wasps that will own the rows by September.

Example

Backstage, the piano tuner's arrival is the harbinger of opening week: he comes exactly nine days out, unhurried, smelling faintly of felt, and after his visit the building never quite empties again. The tuner sells no tickets and hangs no lights. He matters to the company because of what his coming announces — everything that follows him now follows on a schedule.

Harbinger is the exact word because a harbinger is a sign that something is coming — it arrives first and announces, without being the event or even causing it. The wasps do not come because the apples fell, exactly; but where the one appears, the other reliably follows.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

herald: A herald announces what approaches, and the word keeps a whiff of the royal messenger sent ahead on purpose. A harbinger merely appears — first frost, first falling leaf — and the announcing lies in our reading of it. Heralds are sent; harbingers just show up.

omen: An omen is a sign read for fate, good or ill — it belongs to superstition, and someone must interpret it. A harbinger is the practical early sign of something reliably on its way: no fate, no reading, just the arrival that announces the rest.

bellwether: A bellwether is the lead member of the crowd itself — the first sheep through the gate, the county whose vote tracks the nation's. It belongs to what it predicts. A harbinger stands apart from what it announces, arriving ahead of an event it is no part of.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

aftermath: what is left once it has happened

echo: a trace that follows, not foretells

Where it sits · how certain the arrival is — hint → harbinger → guarantee

hint vs. harbinger: A hint is the faintest rung — a trace you could miss or explain away, far milder than a harbinger.

guarantee vs. harbinger: A guarantee goes further than a harbinger: a harbinger announces that something is likely on its way, while a guarantee promises it cannot fail to arrive.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — harbing-

Root — harbing-: lodging, shelter for an army (Old French herberge — Middle English reshaped the vowels and slipped in the n on the way to harbinger)

Suffix — -er

Suffix — -er: one who

Put it together

Put it together: Harbing- (lodging, army shelter — Old French herberge, reshaped by Middle English, which slipped in the n) + -er (one who) = the one who arranges the lodging. A medieval harbinger rode ahead of a royal party to secure rooms for the night — so his appearance in your village meant exactly one thing: the court itself was on the road behind him. The job vanished; the announcing stayed.

Use the root in a new word: harbor

Use the root in a new word: harbor: The fleet rode out the gale inside the harbor's stone arms.

Strength Check

Word Choice

literary / journalistic

Harbinger is the writer's word for the early sign — first frost, first moving van, first quiet resignation. It looks forward: the harbinger arrives, the thing follows. Its unit-mate antecedent runs the other way, found by looking back from a thing to what led toward it. Use omen when the reading is superstition, bellwether when the sign is the first member of the crowd itself.
